question.question:
D1 — Retry mechanism: reuse the job library's retry hooks or build a custom inline scheduler?
Project/branch/task: main, "Add background job retry framework" plan review; repo holds only PLAN.md, so this is judged on the plan text.
ELI10: The plan rebuilds retry scheduling inside every worker even though the job library already has retry hooks that do the same thing. The stated reason is wanting control over the backoff curve, but libraries in this class let you hand them your own backoff function, so you keep the curve and drop the rebuild. A custom scheduler also has to re-solve things the library already handles: remembering how many attempts happened, surviving a worker crash mid-wait, and showing up in the library's dashboards.
Stakes if we pick wrong: a hand-rolled scheduler means five places where attempt counting or delay math can drift, retries lost when a worker restarts, and a retry framework nobody else on the team recognizes. Picking the library when its hooks turn out to lack a needed feature costs a day of rework, which option C removes.
Recommendation: A because the plan's only reason to leave the library ("full control over the curve") is met by a custom backoff function, so the rebuild buys nothing and costs persistence, observability and five maintenance sites.
Completeness: A=9/10, B=5/10, C=n/a (investigation only, approves nothing)
Pros / cons:
A) Library hooks + custom backoff function (recommended)
  ✅ Attempt count, delay persistence and crash recovery stay library-owned; nothing to re-implement per worker
  ✅ The backoff curve is still fully yours: one function returns the delay for attempt N (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20 min)
  ✅ Finding 2 (five copy-pasted envelopes) disappears: the envelope is config, not worker code
  ❌ Depends on the library's hook API actually accepting a custom backoff function; not verified here because the library is not in this repo
B) Custom inline scheduler per worker (as planned)
  ✅ Zero dependency on the library's hook surface; works even if its hooks are rigid
  ✅ Lets each worker tune its curve independently without touching queue config
  ❌ Each worker must own attempt tracking, timers and restart recovery; a crash mid-backoff silently drops the retry unless you also build persistence (human: ~3 days / CC: ~1 h)
  ❌ Keeps the five-copy duplication alive and puts the retry path outside the library's metrics and dashboards
C) Investigate the hook API first, then decide
  ✅ Replaces the unverified assumption in A with a 5-minute read of the library's retry/backoff hook docs or source
  ✅ Costs almost nothing and makes the A/B call on evidence instead of plan text
  ❌ Defers the decision; nothing in this plan can be approved until the read-back is done
Net: trade an unverified hook-API assumption (A) against a known rebuild of persistence, observability and five maintenance sites (B); C buys the evidence for a few minutes.

question.question:
D2 — Webhook delivery: what guarantee do receivers get once `processWebhookJob()` can retry?
Project/branch/task: main, "Add background job retry framework"; R1 settled on the library's retry hooks, now the webhook flow's semantics.
ELI10: Today a webhook is sent at most once: if it fails, it is gone, but a receiver never sees the same event twice. The moment you add retries, a request that timed out after reaching the receiver gets sent again, and the receiver sees a duplicate. You have to pick on purpose: embrace duplicates and give receivers a key to spot them, only retry when you are sure the request never left, or keep webhooks out of the retry framework entirely.
Stakes if we pick wrong: silently flipping to at-least-once means customers' systems double-charge, double-notify or double-create records with no way to detect it. Keeping at-most-once means the common failure (a 5xx or a slow receiver) still loses the event.
Recommendation: A because at-least-once with a documented idempotency key is the standard webhook contract and the only option that both recovers lost deliveries and lets receivers protect themselves.
Completeness: A=9/10, B=6/10, C=4/10
Pros / cons:
A) At-least-once with idempotency key (recommended)
  ✅ Recovers deliveries lost to 5xx and read timeouts, which is most of what a retry framework exists for
  ✅ Receivers get a stable key per event and a documented "may deliver more than once" contract they can dedupe on (human: ~1.5 days / CC: ~30 min)
  ❌ Changes the receiver-facing contract; any receiver that does not dedupe will see duplicates until they do
B) Retry only pre-send failures
  ✅ Preserves the current at-most-once guarantee exactly; no receiver sees a duplicate
  ✅ Still recovers the cheap failures (connection refused, DNS, TLS handshake) with no contract change (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20 min)
  ❌ The most common failures (5xx, slow receiver) stay lost, and classifying "provably never sent" per HTTP client is brittle
C) Exclude the webhook flow from retries
  ✅ Zero contract risk and almost zero work; the other four workers still get retries (human: ~0 / CC: ~2 min)
  ✅ Buys time to decide the webhook contract with receivers separately
  ❌ The webhook flow gets no reliability gain from this change, and the plan's rewrite of `processWebhookJob()` would need to be dropped
Net: trade a documented contract change that receivers must honor (A) against preserving at-most-once at the cost of still losing the common failures (B, C).

Receiver-facing docs updated to "at-least-once, dedupe on the key". Human ~1.5 days / CC ~30 min. Completeness 9/10. R3 regression contract stays pending.

options.label: Retry only pre-send failures
options.description: Retry only when the request provably never left (connection refused, DNS, TLS handshake failure); read timeouts and 5xx are terminal. Preserves at-most-once. Each attempt recorded. Human ~1 day / CC ~20 min. Completeness 6/10: 5xx and slow receivers still lose the event. R3 stays pending.

options.label: Exclude the webhook flow from retries

question.question:
D3 — Jitter: randomize retry delays, or keep the pure exponential curve?
Project/branch/task: main, "Add background job retry framework"; the curve now lives in one custom backoff function supplied to the library hooks (D1).
ELI10: If a downstream service goes down for a minute, hundreds of jobs fail at the same moment. With a pure exponential curve they all wake up and retry at the same instants, hammering the service just as it recovers. Jitter adds randomness to each delay so the retries spread out instead of arriving as a wave.
Stakes if we pick wrong: without jitter the first retry wave after an outage can knock the dependency over again and extend the incident; with jitter the only cost is that a given retry may fire a little earlier or later than the textbook curve.
Recommendation: A because full jitter is the documented safe default for background jobs, it is a one-line change inside the backoff function, and every real-world retry-storm bug found in research traced back to its absence.
Completeness: A=9/10, B=8/10, C=4/10
Pros / cons:
A) Full jitter (recommended)
  ✅ Spreads retries across the whole window, the strongest protection against a lockstep wave after a shared outage
  ✅ One line inside the custom backoff function; no new state, no new dependency (human: ~1 h incl. test / CC: ~3 min)
  ❌ A retry can fire almost immediately after a failure (random lower bound is 0), which can look surprising in logs
B) Equal jitter
  ✅ Guarantees a minimum wait of half the computed delay, so no retry fires "too soon"
  ✅ Still breaks up the lockstep wave, just over half the window (human: ~1 h incl. test / CC: ~3 min)
  ❌ Weaker spread than full jitter; only worth it if a hard minimum wait is a real requirement here, and none is stated
C) No jitter (as planned)
  ✅ Delays are exactly predictable, which makes the curve easy to reason about and test
  ✅ Zero extra code beyond the curve itself
  ❌ Every job that failed in the same outage retries at the same instants; this is the classic retry-storm bug reported against real queue libraries
Net: a few minutes of code (A or B) against a known outage amplifier (C); A unless a hard minimum wait is a stated requirement.

options.label: Full jitter (recommended)
options.description: Custom backoff function returns random(0, base * 2^attempt). One line plus a test asserting delays stay within [0, computed]. Human ~1 h / CC ~3 min. Completeness 9/10. R6 cap, R7 max attempts/dead-letter stay pending.

options.label: Equal jitter
options.description: Custom backoff function returns computed/2 + random(0, computed/2). Guaranteed minimum wait. One line plus a bounds test. Human ~1 h / CC ~3 min. Completeness 8/10. R6, R7 stay pending.

options.label: No jitter (as planned)
options.description: Custom backoff function returns base * 2^attempt exactly. Lockstep retries after a shared outage are accepted. Human ~0 / CC ~0. Completeness 4/10. R6, R7 stay pending.

We'll roll a custom exponential-backoff scheduler inline in each worker

Question D3:
D3 — Jitter: randomize retry delays, or keep the pure exponential curve?
Project/branch/task: main, "Add background job retry framework"; the curve now lives in one custom backoff function supplied to the library hooks (D1).
ELI10: If a downstream service goes down for a minute, hundreds of jobs fail at the same moment. With a pure exponential curve they all wake up and retry at the same instants, hammering the service just as it recovers. Jitter adds randomness to each delay so the retries spread out instead of arriving as a wave.
Stakes if we pick wrong: without jitter the first retry wave after an outage can knock the dependency over again and extend the incident; with jitter the only cost is that a given retry may fire a little earlier or later than the textbook curve.
Recommendation: A because full jitter is the documented safe default for background jobs, it is a one-line change inside the backoff function, and every real-world retry-storm bug found in research traced back to its absence.
Completeness: A=9/10, B=8/10, C=4/10
Pros / cons:
A) Full jitter (recommended)
  ✅ Spreads retries across the whole window, the strongest protection against a lockstep wave after a shared outage
  ✅ One line inside the custom backoff function; no new state, no new dependency (human: ~1 h incl. test / CC: ~3 min)
  ❌ A retry can fire almost immediately after a failure (random lower bound is 0), which can look surprising in logs
B) Equal jitter
  ✅ Guarantees a minimum wait of half the computed delay, so no retry fires "too soon"
  ✅ Still breaks up the lockstep wave, just over half the window (human: ~1 h incl. test / CC: ~3 min)
  ❌ Weaker spread than full jitter; only worth it if a hard minimum wait is a real requirement here, and none is stated
C) No jitter (as planned)
  ✅ Delays are exactly predictable, which makes the curve easy to reason about and test
  ✅ Zero extra code beyond the curve itself
  ❌ Every job that failed in the same outage retries at the same instants; this is the classic retry-storm bug reported against real queue libraries
Net: a few minutes of code (A or B) against a known outage amplifier (C); A unless a hard minimum wait is a stated requirement.
